body.estimand_functional: \(Q=\mathsf{Rec}^{(1)}_{T,k,j,B}((M_d)_{d=0}^T)\) when \(S_k=\{j\}\), \(S_t=\varnothing\) for \(t\ne k\), and \(\mathsf C_1(T,k,j,B,(|\mathcal X_t|)_{t=1}^T)=1\)

sampling_model.design: Known randomized second-stage audit within each dropout stratum, with a fixed bundle \(B_d\) and probability \(e_d(H_d)\).
sampling_model.units: Independent records \(O_1,\ldots,O_n\) from the positive finite SCM class.
sampling_model.treatment: Observational treatment \(A\) has a strictly positive conditional law given \(W\); intervention replaces that kernel by \(A=a\).
sampling_model.overlap: All substantive table entries and all legal continuation and audit probabilities are strictly positive.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Use empirical observed-cell frequencies or Horvitz--Thompson audit-pattern tables with known \(e_d\); on a successful single-hazard design, apply the deterministic rational reconstruction selected by \(\mathsf A_1\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Monotonicity permits several response-kernel recoveries yet a mediated self-censoring path makes the corresponding marginal and target laws nonidentified.
A categorical colluder propensity is identified if and only if its observable colluder matrices have full column rank.
Randomized intensive follow-up identifies and efficiently estimates smooth complete-data functionals when the phase-two variables complete the coarsened record.
In ordinary nonmonotone missing-data DAGs, absence of self-censoring and colluder obstructions characterizes full-law identification.
A sound intervention tree yields constructive target-law identification but is not complete.
Finite discrete causal queries admit sharp bounds through polynomial programming and convergent branch-and-bound.

body.tldr: For the complete arbitrary-horizon subclass with exactly one substantively informative continuation hazard, a finite audit-incidence scan is necessary and sufficient for identifying the entire endpoint intervention distribution. A successful scan returns an explicit rational reconstruction from one audited pre-hazard dropout marginal, a risk-set mixture when needed, and a complete-case Markov tail; a failed scan returns two strictly positive graph-compatible SCMs with identical observed laws and different endpoint interventions. The exact minimal frontier contains \(k(T-j+1)\) singleton audit designs. Empirical plug-in estimation is smooth at every positive law, while observed-cell projection retains finite-sample coverage beyond identified designs. Interacting multi-hazard completeness is left to future work.

project_justification.gap: Passive monotone-MNAR theory gives local recovery formulas and self-censoring obstructions, while randomized double-sampling theory typically completes the missing record. Neither gives a necessary-and-sufficient partial-audit rule for the endpoint intervention distribution in an arbitrary-horizon chain with one current- or lead-state-dependent hazard.
project_justification.niche: The single-informative-hazard graph family is broad in horizon, alphabet sizes, audit bundles, null allowed-arrow effects, and transition rank, yet its response fiber admits a complete incidence alternative with an explicit positive obstruction.
project_justification.fill: A finite scan of \(\mathcal H(B)=\{(d,\ell):d<k,\ell\ge j,\ell\in B_d\}\) returns either a rational endpoint reconstruction or a strictly positive observational-equivalence witness, proves \(\mathsf C_1=\operatorname{GID}\) on this complete subclass, and enumerates all \(k(T-j+1)\) minimal designs.

body.related_work: Tikka and Karvanen (2025) establish monotone-missingness recoveries and a mediated self-censoring nonidentification construction, but do not decide which same-subject partial audits identify an endpoint intervention distribution. The present theorem closes that audit-design question for the arbitrary-horizon single-informative-hazard subclass, not for interacting local hazards. Tikka and Karvanen (2024) study rank conditions for categorical colluder propensities; the present reconstruction uses no transition-rank premise. Levis et al. (2024) identify smooth complete-data functionals after randomized intensive follow-up that completes the coarsened record, whereas the sufficient singleton audits here may recover neither the full trajectory nor the endpoint. Guo and Nabi (2026) give a sound intervention-tree construction without the completeness claim made here for this restricted graph family. Duarte et al. (2024) supply finite polynomial optimization machinery used only for projected confidence sets, not for the graph-explicit incidence theorem.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The theorem is complete only for graphs with one substantively informative hazard \(S_k=\{j\}\), \(j\in\{k,k+1\}\), and all other \(S_t\) empty. It does not assert that this graph family is inclusion-maximal. Interacting hazards can create overlapping-parent constraints, positive-scaling recoveries on singular strata, alphabet-sensitive bridges, endpoint-only cancellations, and countermodel-gluing problems not addressed by the finite incidence scan; an arbitrary-local-graph recovery-or-obstruction calculus, its termination proof, and its positive gluing theorem remain future work.
body.honest_scope: The completed field claim is an arbitrary-horizon necessary-and-sufficient design theorem for the full single-informative-hazard subclass. It covers every specified finite alphabet with at least two states per visit, every positive substantive and response law, null effects on allowed arrows, and deficient transition ranks. It supplies an evaluable reconstruction, a legal positive countermodel on failure, and the exact minimal frontier, but makes no claim for graphs with two or more substantively informative hazards and no claim that the subclass is inclusion-maximal. No shadow-variable rank, parametric selection, missing-at-random, or faithfulness assumption is imposed, and no polynomial-time guarantee is claimed. Global projected confidence sets remain valid for all designs, including insufficient ones.
